lessons.title: Body systems of the horse and common ailments
lessons.html:
Knowing the healthy horse

You cannot spot illness unless you know what normal looks like. Learn the main body systems and the normal resting values for an adult horse.

SystemMain parts and function
DigestiveSmall stomach, long small intestine, large caecum and colon that ferment fibre. Horses cannot vomit.
RespiratoryNostrils, larynx, trachea, lungs. Horses breathe only through the nose.
CirculatoryHeart, blood vessels; pulse felt under the jaw.
MusculoskeletalBones, joints, tendons, ligaments and hooves for movement.
Nervous, skin, urinary, reproductive and immuneControl, protection, waste removal, breeding and defence.

Normal resting values (adult)

  • Temperature: about 37.5 to 38.5 °C
  • Heart rate: about 28 to 44 beats per minute
  • Breathing: about 8 to 16 breaths per minute
  • Gums: moist and salmon pink, capillary refill under 2 seconds

Common ailments

  • Colic: abdominal pain. Signs include pawing, rolling, looking at the flanks, sweating and no dung. Call the vet at once; remove feed and keep the horse safe while you wait. Do not give medicine unless the vet tells you to.
  • Laminitis: painful inflammation in the hoof, often after too much rich grass or grain. The horse leans back to take weight off its front feet. It is an emergency.
  • Thrush: black, smelly infection of the frog. Prevent with clean, dry bedding and daily hoof picking.
  • Mud fever and rain scald: skin infections in wet conditions.
  • Wounds: clean gently with clean water and get vet help for deep wounds, wounds near joints, or puncture wounds in the hoof.
  • Dental problems: dropping feed (quidding) and weight loss; teeth need routine checks and rasping by a vet or equine dentist.

lessons.title: Infectious diseases and immunity
lessons.html:
How infectious diseases spread

Infectious diseases are caused by germs: bacteria, viruses and protozoa. They spread through direct contact, shared buckets and tack, the air, insects and ticks, or contaminated soil.

Important diseases in South Africa

DiseaseCauseSpread and control
African horse sicknessVirusCarried by Culicoides midges, worst in late summer and autumn. A controlled disease: vaccinate as required by law and your vet, stable horses at dusk and dawn, use insect repellent.
Equine influenzaVirusSpread by coughing and contact. Vaccination and isolation.
StranglesBacteria (Streptococcus equi)Abscesses under the jaw. Highly contagious; isolate, strict hygiene, vet treatment.
TetanusBacteria in soilEnters through wounds. Prevent by vaccination.
Biliary (piroplasmosis)Protozoa in red blood cellsSpread by ticks. Fever, yellow gums, dark urine. Tick control and vet treatment.
RabiesVirusBite of an infected animal; dangerous to people. Report suspicion to the state vet.

Diseases such as African horse sickness are controlled under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984, and suspected cases must be reported to the state veterinarian.

How immunity works

The immune system recognises germs and makes antibodies and memory cells that fight them next time.

  • Active immunity: the horse makes its own antibodies after infection or vaccination. It lasts months to years; boosters keep it high.
  • Passive immunity: ready-made antibodies received, mainly by the foal from colostrum (first milk) in the first hours of life. It protects only for a few months.

Vaccines must be stored in the fridge as stated on the label, given by the correct route and recorded in the horse's passport or health record.

lessons.title: Implementing a vet-directed treatment programme
lessons.html:
Working under the vet's direction

The veterinarian diagnoses and prescribes. Your job is to carry out the treatment exactly, observe the horse and report back. Many medicines are scheduled and may only be used as prescribed.

Before treatment

  1. Read the vet's written instructions: medicine, dose, route (mouth, muscle, skin, eye), frequency and duration.
  2. Check the label: name, strength, expiry date and storage conditions.
  3. Identify the right horse by name, markings and microchip or brand.
  4. Prepare a safe area and a handler to hold the horse.

During treatment

  • Use clean equipment and new needles; never reuse needles between horses.
  • Give oral paste at the corner of the mouth onto the back of the tongue, then hold the head up briefly.
  • Only give injections if you have been trained and the vet has instructed you.
  • Stand to the side of the horse, never directly behind.

After treatment

  • Record the date, time, medicine, dose, batch number and who gave it.
  • Watch for reactions such as swelling, sweating, colic or breathing trouble and call the vet if they occur.
  • Complete the full course, even if the horse looks better.
  • Dispose of needles in a sharps container.
  • Follow the withdrawal period stated on the label before a horse competes or races, because of doping rules.

Routine programme

With the vet, plan a yearly calendar: vaccinations, deworming based on faecal egg counts, tick control, dental checks and hoof care.

Key points

  • Know normal temperature, pulse and breathing so you can spot illness.
  • Colic and laminitis are emergencies: call the vet at once.
  • African horse sickness is spread by midges; vaccinate and stable at dusk and dawn.
  • Vaccination gives active immunity; colostrum gives the foal passive immunity.
  • Follow the vet's instructions exactly and record every treatment.
